prompt: Before rebutting a colleague's plan, an engineer says, 'Let me make sure I have your strongest argument: you think speed now beats a cleaner design because the market window is short. Right?'
tells: 'Let me make sure I have your strongest argument
why: Restate their best case before replying.
trap: She isn't agreeing yet; she's checking she understands.

prompt: A director plays devil's advocate against a proposal. The presenter repeats the objection back in its best form and asks if that's the concern before answering.
tells: repeats the objection back in its best form
why: Showing you understand the objection makes your answer land.
trap: He may still hold his ground after; the move here is restating.

prompt: In a debate about remote work, a manager catches himself mocking a weak version of the other side, and instead says the most reasonable version of their case out loud.
tells: says the most reasonable version of their case out loud
trap: He's not giving in; he's being fair to their case.

prompt: In a system design interview, the interviewer argues for a single database. The candidate says, 'So the case is that one database is simpler to run and our scale doesn't need more. Is that it?' before responding.
tells: 'So the case is that one database is simpler to run and our scale doesn't need more. Is that it?'
why: Restate the pushback fairly, then answer.
trap: They haven't agreed or disagreed yet.

prompt: Before a decision meeting, a lead writes a paragraph making the opposing team's case as well as they would, and sends it to them to check.
tells: making the opposing team's case as well as they would
why: Show you understand the other side at its best.
trap: It isn't uncovering needs; it's presenting their argument fairly.

prompt: In an interview, a candidate says that when they disagree, they first summarize the other person's view until the person says, 'Yes, exactly.'
why: Prove you understand before you argue.
trap: It's about disagreement, not receiving feedback.
